name: LEGO Minifigure Animation Short
description: Develops a theme, characters, scenes, conflict or reference assets into a LEGO Minifigure style animated short, advancing in stages through the script outline, storyboard plan, key element anchoring and single-clip videos, keeping LEGO minifigure proportions, brick scene logic and cross-shot consistency.

planning.planning_notes:
[Stage path]
1. Before starting, judge the entry point from the target duration, aspect ratio, dialogue language, user input and canvas/uploaded assets; when more information is needed, first confirm with the user the theme, characters, scenes, conflict, emotion, target audience and asset availability.
2. From the confirmed information, generate a Logline and a three-act script outline, and make this stage's output clear and reviewable.
3. From the script outline and the confirmed information, generate Key Elements and a three-level Sequence -> Shot Group -> Shot storyboard, and make this stage's output clear and reviewable.
4. After the storyboard plan is complete, enter the visual key element stage: first list from the Key Elements the independent assets that need to be reused across shots, and create a separate draft node for each asset. One node for each recurring protagonist or important character; one node for each main scene reused by multiple shots; one node for each core prop, vehicle or creature that needs a consistent appearance. Bind the user's existing assets first, and only generate the corresponding node when missing. Do not create just one generic "visual key elements" node, and do not merge multiple independently referenceable characters, scenes or props into one overview image; only assets that are always referenced downstream as one whole may share a node. Make each key element output clear and reviewable.
5. After the key elements are complete, generate video clips per Shot Group or single Shot; each video clip references only the character, scene and prop element images it actually needs, usually skipping the previous shot's video reference and using it only for strongly continuous action.
6. Final editing and export are handled by the canvas compose node.

[Planning rules]
The aspect ratio, target duration and dialogue language confirmed before starting must run through the storyboard, key element and video stages.
A Shot Group revolves around a single narrative goal, usually 8-15 seconds and 3-8 Shots; a Shot must serve the narrative logic, without piling on meaningless camera movement.
planning.prompt_guide:
All stage outputs use Markdown in the same language as the user's input, unless the user explicitly asks for another language.

[LEGO visual language]
The core style is locked to LEGO Minifigure animation: official LEGO minifigure proportions, ABS plastic material, printed faces, brick hands, short-leg proportions, cinematic lighting, and a clear, high-quality toy photography look. Realistic human proportions, Anime long-body proportions, non-brick toy styles and organic realistic materials are forbidden.

[Brick scene language]
All scene elements follow LEGO building logic: buildings, roads, furniture, vehicles, trees, water and props are all built from brick geometry; avoid real organic curved structures. Scene descriptions must state the building layout, roads, key prop positions, time of day and light direction.

[Prompt expression]
Image prompts write only what is visible in the picture, focusing on locking hairstyle, clothing colors and patterns, accessories, printed faces, scene spatial relationships and key prop positions. Video prompts are organized as Subject description -> Action beats -> Scene and environment -> Shot scale + camera movement -> Lighting effects -> style anchoring; dialogue uses {original dialogue} and sound effects use <sound effect description>.
conduct_rules: Create the complete workflow draft first; the output of each main stage must be clear and reviewable, and the actual pace of continuing, retrying and executing is controlled by the canvas workflow.

Before starting, the theme, characters, scenes, conflict, emotion, target audience and availability of existing assets must be confirmed; this information serves as the planning basis and does not create extra stages of its own.
The confirmed duration, aspect ratio, language and LEGO visual style must run through the storyboard, key element and video stages.
All characters must keep LEGO Minifigure proportions and the official LEGO minifigure style; realistic human proportions, Anime proportions or non-brick toy styles are forbidden.
All scenes must follow LEGO building logic and avoid real organic curved structures.

Once confirmed, key elements become the appearance anchors for the whole film; all later shots must reuse the corresponding character and scene elements and must not change hairstyle, clothing, accessories, printed faces or scene spatial relationships on their own.

The key element stage must not create just one generic "visual key elements" node. Every recurring protagonist or important character, every main reused scene, and every core prop/vehicle/creature that needs a consistent appearance across shots must be its own node; do not replace multiple independent elements with one overview image.
If the user has already uploaded matching character or scene assets, they must be registered and bound to the corresponding Key Element first, rather than regenerated.
Shot design must use the three-level Sequence -> Shot Group -> Shot structure; each Shot Group revolves around one narrative goal.

Every Shot must contain shot scale, camera movement, visualizable character actions, the complete original dialogue and sound effect notes; designing on-screen subtitles or floating text at the Shot level is forbidden.
Action descriptions may only write visualizable actions and must not substitute invisible psychological states such as "falls into thought" or "feels pain" for the picture.

Video shots must bind the relevant character element images and scene element images; the previous shot's video serves as a reference only in strongly continuous action scenes, and is usually skipped to avoid style drift.
Final editing, mixing and export are handled by the canvas compose node.

rating_bands.description: The stages are clearly separated with complete stage boundaries, and LEGO minifigure proportions, brick scene logic, key element consistency, three-level storyboard and the final quality check all land stably in the outputs.
The flow is basically complete, but some stages lack asset analysis, element locking, the three-level storyboard, shot fields or stage boundaries.
Stages are skipped, stage boundaries are muddled, realistic human/anime proportions are used, scenes do not follow brick logic, or key element binding and subtitle rules are ignored.

visual_review_items.name: LEGO minifigure style
visual_review_items.description: Characters must have official LEGO Minifigure proportions, ABS plastic texture, printed faces, brick hands and short-leg proportions.

visual_review_items.name: Brick scene logic
visual_review_items.description: Scenes, props, vehicles, roads and natural elements all conform to brick-built geometry, with no realistic organic structures.

visual_review_items.name: Cross-shot consistency
visual_review_items.description: Hairstyle, clothing colors, patterns, accessories, printed faces and scene spatial relationships stay consistent across all shots.

text_review_items.name: Stage boundaries
text_review_items.description: Each main stage has a clear output, input dependencies and next step, making it easy to review and advance the canvas workflow.

text_review_items.name: Storyboard executability
text_review_items.description: The storyboard has a Sequence/Shot Group/Shot hierarchy, every shot has complete fields, visualizable actions, and dialogue and sound effects that can be executed directly.

domain_constraints: Follow the aspect ratio, target duration and dialogue language chosen before starting.
Characters must be in LEGO Minifigure style; realistic human or Anime proportions must not be used.
Scenes must follow LEGO building logic.
Once confirmed, key elements must be reused as anchors for the whole film.
No subtitles or floating text at the Shot level.
Video clips must bind the relevant character element images and scene element images.
